plan: SAT R&W batch 74: 20 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000684..000703 (9 SEC: Marian Anderson comma+and, Ella Fitzgerald agreement, Bessie Smith plural, Homo naledi modifier, pykrete colon, pitcher plant compound subject, foxfire whose, elephant infrasound dash, Chicxulub evidence agreement; Hubble Deep Field and Halley 1910 WIC; Angkor lidar structure; Hagia Sophia purpose; Foote/Tyndall cross-text; Phoenician alphabet inference; paper airplane two-part data; Taj Mahal particle evidence; Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson transitions; Gladys West synthesis). Topics checked against both workstreams. Plus S073-06 (antecedent rewritten) and S073-15 (passage states higher prices) as revision 2 on previously unbanked passages. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A concert on the steps
passages.text: In 1939, the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let the singer Marian Anderson perform at Constitution Hall in Washington, D.C., because she was Black. In protest, first lady Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the ______ Anderson instead sang on Easter Sunday from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial to a crowd of about 75,000 people.

passages.title: The songbook recordings
passages.text: Over her long career, Ella Fitzgerald recorded more than 200 albums. Her "songbook" recordings from the 1950s and 1960s, each devoted to the work of a single composer such as Cole Porter or Duke Ellington, ______ widely regarded as definitive versions of many American popular songs.

passages.title: Empress of the Blues
passages.text: Known as the "Empress of the Blues," Bessie Smith was among the best-selling recording ______ of the 1920s, and her powerful voice influenced generations of later singers.

passages.title: Bones in the dark
passages.text: In 2013, cavers exploring the Rising Star cave system in South Africa squeezed through a narrow passage into a chamber scattered with fossil bones. Recovered and studied over the following years, ______

passages.title: Ships of ice
passages.text: During World War II, British planners studied an unusual building ______ a frozen mixture of water and wood pulp called pykrete, which was stronger than ordinary ice and melted far more slowly.

passages.title: A slippery trap
passages.text: Pitcher plants catch insects in tube-shaped leaves partly filled with digestive fluid. Insects drawn to the nectar around the opening often lose their footing and fall in. The slippery rim and the waxy inner walls of the leaf ______ them from climbing back out.

passages.title: A glow in the woods
passages.text: For centuries, people walking through forests at night noticed a faint green glow coming from decaying logs, which they called foxfire. Scientists now know that the light comes from certain fungi, ______ glow results from a chemical reaction involving an enzyme called luciferase.

passages.title: Rumbles below hearing
passages.text: In the 1980s, the biologist Katy Payne discovered that elephants communicate in part through ______ low-pitched rumbles below the range of human hearing that can travel several kilometers.

passages.title: Evidence of an impact
passages.text: Rocks around the world contain a thin layer that dates to about 66 million years ago, when most dinosaurs disappeared. Evidence from these rocks, including the layer's unusually high levels of the element iridium, ______ that a large asteroid struck Earth at that time, near what is now the Yucatán Peninsula.

passages.title: A crowded patch of sky
passages.text: In 1995, astronomers pointed the Hubble Space Telescope for ten days at a tiny patch of sky that appeared nearly empty. The resulting image, known as the Hubble Deep Field, revealed roughly 3,000 galaxies, showing that the seemingly blank region was in fact ______ with distant objects.

passages.title: Comet pills
passages.text: As Earth prepared to pass through the tail of Halley's comet in 1910, newspapers reported that astronomers had detected a poisonous gas in the tail. Although scientists explained that the gas was far too thin to cause harm, the reports caused ______ in some places, and enterprising sellers marketed "comet pills" to anxious buyers.

passages.title: A city beneath the forest
passages.text: For more than a century, visitors to Angkor Wat in Cambodia admired its towering stone temples, which were built in the 1100s. Much less was known about the city that had surrounded them, since its wooden buildings had long since vanished beneath the forest. In 2012, researchers flew over the area using lidar, a technology that uses laser pulses to map the ground beneath trees. The scans revealed a grid of streets, ponds, and mounds where houses had once stood, showing that the temples had been the center of a large city.

passages.title: Who measured the heat first?
passages.text:
Text 1
The Irish physicist John Tyndall is often credited as the first to show that certain gases, including carbon dioxide and water vapor, absorb heat. His careful laboratory measurements, begun in 1859, became a foundation of climate science.

Text 2
In 1856, the American scientist Eunice Foote reported experiments in which glass cylinders filled with carbon dioxide grew warmer in sunlight than cylinders filled with ordinary air. She suggested that more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere would make Earth warmer. Her paper was read at a scientific meeting by a male colleague, Joseph Henry.

passages.title: One building, many roles
passages.text: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul was completed in 537 as a cathedral for the Byzantine emperor Justinian. After the Ottoman conquest of the city in 1453, it was converted into a mosque, and minarets were added around it. In 1934, the Turkish government turned the building into a museum, and in 2020 it was designated a mosque once again.

passages.title: Twenty-two letters
passages.text: Early writing systems such as Egyptian hieroglyphs and Mesopotamian cuneiform used hundreds of different signs, and mastering them typically took years of training. By about 1050 BCE, the Phoenicians, a trading people of the eastern Mediterranean, were using an alphabet of just 22 letters, each standing for a consonant sound. Phoenician merchants carried the alphabet across the Mediterranean, where it was adopted and adapted by others, including the Greeks. This history suggests that ______

passages.title: Paper airplanes
passages.text:
A student tested three paper airplane designs, throwing each one five times.
Dart: average distance 6.1 m; longest throw 9.0 m
Glider: average distance 8.4 m; longest throw 8.9 m
Stunt: average distance 4.0 m; longest throw 5.2 m
The student claims that although the dart produced the single longest throw, the glider flew farther on average.

passages.title: A yellowing monument
passages.text: The white marble of the Taj Mahal in Agra, India, has gradually taken on a yellowish-brown tint. Researchers hypothesize that particles of air pollution settling on the marble, rather than any change within the stone itself, are mainly responsible for the discoloration.

passages.title: Learning the new machines
passages.text: In the late 1950s, the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, which later became NASA, began using electronic computers, and many of the human "computers" it employed to do calculations by hand worried about their jobs. Dorothy Vaughan, who supervised a group of Black women mathematicians at the Langley laboratory in Virginia, saw the change coming. ______ she taught herself and her staff the programming language FORTRAN, preparing them to work with the new machines.

passages.title: A petition to learn
passages.text: Mary Jackson, a mathematician at NASA's Langley laboratory in Virginia, wanted to become an engineer, but some of the courses she needed were taught at a high school in Hampton, Virginia, that was then open only to white students. ______ she petitioned the city for permission to attend. The request was granted, and in 1958 she became NASA's first Black female engineer.

passages.title: Notes on a mathematician
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Gladys West began working as a mathematician at the Naval Surface Warfare Center in Dahlgren, Virginia, in 1956.
- She programmed computers to build an extremely precise mathematical model of Earth's shape using satellite data.
- Models like hers are needed for the Global Positioning System (GPS) to calculate locations accurately.
- Many people now use GPS every day on their phones.
- In 2018, she was inducted into the U.S. Air Force Space and Missile Pioneers Hall of Fame.

passages.title: A light to hide by
passages.text: The Hawaiian bobtail squid hunts in shallow water at night, when moonlight could cast its shadow onto the sand below. To hide that shadow, the squid relies on light from Vibrio fischeri bacteria, which ______ in dense colonies inside a special organ on its underside.

passages.title: A potter's signature
passages.text: Maria Martinez, a potter from San Ildefonso Pueblo in New Mexico, became famous for her polished black-on-black pottery, which she developed with her husband, Julian, around 1918. As collectors' interest grew in the 1920s, she began signing her pots, and signed pieces soon drew higher prices than unsigned ones. Martinez sometimes also signed pots that had been made by other women of the pueblo. This practice suggests that ______

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Anderson instead sang on Easter Sunday
candidates.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by a comma followed by the coordinating conjunction "and."

A.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

B.rationale: The comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from its clause.

D.rationale: A semicolon followed by "and" and a comma is not a standard way to join these clauses.

hints: Can both parts stand alone as sentences?

strategy.explanation: Find where the first clause ends.

candidates.remember: Join independent clauses with a comma plus a conjunction.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Her "songbook" recordings from the 1950s and 1960s
candidates.explanation: The subject is "recordings," which is plural, so it takes "are"; the phrase between the commas does not change the subject.

B.rationale: The subject is the plural "recordings," not "composer."

C.rationale: The singular verb does not agree with the plural "recordings."

D.rationale: "Being" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

hints: Which noun is the subject: "recordings" or "composer"?

strategy.explanation: Cross out the phrase between the commas.

candidates.remember: Agree the verb with its subject, not the nearest noun.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: her powerful voice influenced generations of later singers
candidates.explanation: "Among" requires a plural noun, and nothing is possessed, so the plain plural "artists" is correct.

A.rationale: "Artist's" is singular possessive, but nothing follows that the artist possesses.

B.rationale: "Artists'" is plural possessive, but nothing follows that the artists possess.

C.rationale: "Among the best-selling recording artist" needs a plural noun after "among."

hints: Does anything belong to the noun in the blank?

strategy.explanation: Decide plural or possessive.

candidates.remember: Use an apostrophe only to show possession.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: researchers identified a previously unknown human relative, now called Homo naledi.
choices.B: the bones revealed a previously unknown human relative, now called Homo naledi.
choices.C: a previously unknown human relative, now called Homo naledi, was identified by researchers.
choices.D: Homo naledi was the name given to a previously unknown human relative by researchers.

candidates.evidence: a chamber scattered with fossil bones
candidates.explanation: The opening phrase describes what was recovered and studied, the bones, so "the bones" must follow it.

A.rationale: The researchers were not recovered and studied; the bones were.

C.rationale: The relative was not recovered from the cave; the bones were.

D.rationale: The name was not recovered and studied; the modifier dangles.

hints: What was recovered and studied?

strategy.explanation: Find the noun the opening phrase describes.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier must be followed by the noun it describes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: a frozen mixture of water and wood pulp called pykrete
candidates.explanation: A colon after the complete clause correctly introduces the phrase that identifies the material.

B.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but what follows is a noun phrase.

C.rationale: "Material that a frozen mixture..." leaves the clause without a verb.

hints: Is what follows the blank a clause or a phrase naming the material?

strategy.explanation: Check what each side of the blank needs.

candidates.remember: A colon can introduce an explanation or example after a complete clause.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The slippery rim and the waxy inner walls of the leaf
candidates.explanation: Two subjects joined by "and" form a plural subject, so the plural "prevent" is needed.

A.rationale: The compound subject "rim and ... walls" is plural.

B.rationale: The singular verb does not agree with the plural compound subject.

D.rationale: "Preventing" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

hints: How many things make up the subject?

strategy.explanation: Find every part of the subject.

candidates.remember: Subjects joined by "and" take a plural verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the light comes from certain fungi
candidates.explanation: The glow belongs to the fungi, so the possessive relative pronoun "whose" is correct; "whose" can refer to things as well as people.

A.rationale: "Who's" means "who is"; "who is glow results" makes no sense.

B.rationale: "Which glow results" is ungrammatical; a possessive is needed.

C.rationale: "Their" creates a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma.

hints: Does the word show possession?

strategy.explanation: Test each choice for possession and structure.

candidates.remember: "Whose" shows possession for people and things.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: low-pitched rumbles below the range of human hearing
candidates.explanation: A dash after the complete clause correctly introduces the phrase that explains what infrasound is.

A.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but what follows is a phrase.

C.rationale: "It is" creates a comma splice between two independent clauses.

D.rationale: "Low-pitched rumbles ... several kilometers" has no main verb, so it would be a fragment.

hints: Is what follows the blank a full sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check what each side of the blank needs.

candidates.remember: A dash can introduce an explanation at the end of a sentence.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Evidence from these rocks
candidates.explanation: The subject "Evidence" is singular, so it takes the singular "suggests"; the phrases in between do not change the subject.

A.rationale: The subject is the singular "Evidence," not "rocks" or "levels."

B.rationale: The plural verb does not agree with the singular "Evidence."

D.rationale: "Suggesting" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

hints: Which word is the subject of the main verb?

strategy.explanation: Cross out the phrases between subject and verb.

candidates.remember: Agree the verb with its subject, not nearby plural nouns.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: revealed roughly 3,000 galaxies
candidates.explanation: Roughly 3,000 galaxies in a tiny patch means the region was full of distant objects, or "teeming" with them.

B.rationale: The image showed about 3,000 galaxies, so the region was crowded, not sparse.

C.rationale: Whether the galaxies are connected is not discussed.

D.rationale: The galaxies were revealed, not hidden.

hints: How many galaxies did the image reveal?

strategy.explanation: Predict "crowded."

candidates.remember: Use specific evidence to confirm the meaning.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: marketed "comet pills" to anxious buyers
candidates.explanation: Anxious buyers seeking protective pills show that the reports caused fear, or "alarm."

A.rationale: Anxious buyers seeking pills show that people were not indifferent.

B.rationale: The text describes anxiety, not amusement.

C.rationale: Buying pills to protect against the gas shows belief, not skepticism.

hints: How did people react to the reports?

strategy.explanation: Predict "fear."

candidates.remember: Use details about people's behavior to infer a feeling.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It argues that Angkor Wat's temples were built far earlier than most historians had assumed.
choices.B: It describes a gap in what was known about a site and then explains how a technology filled it.
choices.C: It compares the building methods used for Angkor Wat's temples with those used for its houses.
choices.D: It describes how forests in Cambodia gradually covered the stone temples of Angkor Wat.

candidates.evidence: In 2012, researchers flew over the area using lidar
candidates.explanation: The text explains that little was known about the city around the temples, then describes how lidar revealed it.

A.rationale: The text gives the 1100s and does not dispute the date.

C.rationale: The text mentions wooden buildings but does not compare building methods.

D.rationale: The temples were visible and admired; the forest covered the wooden city.

hints: What was unknown, and what changed?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence's role.

candidates.remember: Structure answers must match every part of the text, in order.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 about Tyndall?

choices.A: By arguing that Tyndall's laboratory measurements of how gases absorb heat were seriously inaccurate
choices.B: By claiming that Foote, rather than Tyndall, measured how water vapor absorbs heat
choices.C: By noting that Foote reported related findings about carbon dioxide before Tyndall began his work
choices.D: By pointing out that Joseph Henry had actually conducted the experiments that Foote later described

candidates.evidence: In 1856, the American scientist Eunice Foote reported experiments
candidates.explanation: Text 1 calls Tyndall the first; Text 2 describes Foote's related 1856 findings on carbon dioxide, so its author would point to her earlier work.

A.rationale: Text 2 does not criticize Tyndall's measurements.

B.rationale: Text 2 describes Foote's work with carbon dioxide, not water vapor.

D.rationale: Henry read Foote's paper; Text 2 does not say he conducted the experiments.

hints: Which date in Text 2 comes before the date in Text 1?

strategy.explanation: Compare the two dates and the two findings.

candidates.remember: Cross-text questions often hinge on a date or a claim of priority.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To trace how one building's use changed over many centuries
choices.B: To explain how the dome of Hagia Sophia was engineered
choices.C: To argue that Hagia Sophia should remain a museum
choices.D: To compare Hagia Sophia with other buildings in Istanbul

candidates.evidence: in 2020 it was designated a mosque once again
candidates.explanation: The text follows Hagia Sophia from cathedral to mosque to museum and back to mosque.

C.rationale: The text reports changes in use without arguing for one.

hints: What changes from one sentence to the next?

strategy.explanation: Label what each sentence does.

candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the Phoenicians invented writing before the Egyptians did.
choices.B: Greek writing used exactly the same letters as Phoenician writing.
choices.C: merchants were the only people who could read in the ancient world.
choices.D: a small set of letters made writing easier to learn and spread.

candidates.evidence: an alphabet of just 22 letters
candidates.explanation: Older systems needed hundreds of signs and years of training; the 22-letter alphabet was adopted widely, which suggests that its simplicity helped it spread.

A.rationale: The text says hieroglyphs came earlier.

B.rationale: The text says the Greeks adapted the alphabet, not that they kept it unchanged.

C.rationale: The text does not support this sweeping claim.

hints: How does the number of signs compare across the systems?

strategy.explanation: Connect the contrast to the alphabet's spread.

candidates.remember: An inference should follow from the contrast the text sets up.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: The glider averaged 8.4 m, which was more than twice the stunt design's average of 4.0 m.
choices.B: The dart's longest throw was 9.0 m, but the glider averaged 8.4 m to the dart's 6.1 m.
choices.C: The dart's longest throw, 9.0 m, was the longest of any throw by the three designs in the test.
choices.D: The glider's longest throw, 8.9 m, was nearly as long as the dart's longest throw of 9.0 m.

candidates.evidence: although the dart produced the single longest throw, the glider flew farther on average
candidates.explanation: The claim has two parts: the dart had the longest throw (9.0 m), and the glider had the higher average (8.4 m versus 6.1 m). Only this choice supports both.

A.rationale: This compares the glider with the stunt design, not with the dart.

C.rationale: This supports only the first part of the claim.

D.rationale: This compares longest throws, not averages.

hints: How many parts does the claim have?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against both parts.

candidates.remember: A two-part claim needs support for both parts.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (finding that supports a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.A: Discolored marble turned white again once the particles on its surface were removed.
choices.B: The Taj Mahal receives millions of visitors each year, many of whom arrive by road.
choices.C: Marble from the same quarry used to build the Taj Mahal is still used in buildings today.
choices.D: The marble has darkened more on some sides of the building than on others over the years.

candidates.evidence: rather than any change within the stone itself
candidates.explanation: If removing surface particles restores the white color, the discoloration lies in deposits on the surface, not in the stone, as the hypothesis predicts.

B.rationale: This describes visitors but does not show that particles cause the color change.

C.rationale: This says nothing about what causes the discoloration.

D.rationale: Uneven darkening alone does not show that surface particles rather than the stone are responsible.

hints: What result would separate the surface from the stone itself?

strategy.explanation: Look for a result that tests the specific cause.

candidates.remember: The strongest support rules out the competing explanation.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: saw the change coming
candidates.explanation: Because Vaughan anticipated the shift to electronic computers, she prepared her staff, so a transition signaling a fitting response is needed.

A.rationale: Learning FORTRAN follows from seeing the change coming; it does not contrast with it.

B.rationale: Learning FORTRAN is not similar to seeing the change; it is a response to it.

D.rationale: Learning FORTRAN is not an example of seeing the change coming.

hints: Is the final sentence a response to the one before it?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Use "Accordingly" for an action that follows from a situation.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: she petitioned the city for permission to attend
candidates.explanation: Jackson's petition was a reaction to the school's exclusion, so "In response" fits.

A.rationale: Petitioning the city is not similar to the barrier; it is a reaction to it.

B.rationale: The petition is not an example of the school's policy.

C.rationale: The petition does not restate the previous sentence.

hints: How does the petition relate to the problem described before it?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Use "In response" for an action taken because of a situation.

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (connecting work to everyday life)
candidates.stem: The student wants to explain how West's work relates to a technology many people use daily. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2018, Gladys West was inducted into the U.S. Air Force Space and Missile Pioneers Hall of Fame for her work as a mathematician.
choices.B: West's precise model of Earth's shape supports the kind of calculations GPS needs, the system many people use daily on their phones.
choices.C: Gladys West began working as a mathematician at the Naval Surface Warfare Center in Dahlgren, Virginia, in the year 1956.
choices.D: Many people now use the Global Positioning System, often called GPS, every day on the phones that they carry with them.

candidates.evidence: Models like hers are needed for the Global Positioning System (GPS)
candidates.explanation: Only this choice links West's model of Earth's shape to GPS and notes that people use GPS daily.

A.rationale: This describes an honor but does not connect her work to an everyday technology.

C.rationale: This gives when and where she worked, not how her work relates to GPS.

D.rationale: This describes GPS use but does not mention West's work.

hints: Which choice mentions both West's work and GPS?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against both parts of the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must meet every part of the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the squid relies on light from Vibrio fischeri bacteria
candidates.explanation: The relative pronoun "which" refers to "bacteria," which is plural, so the verb is "live."

A.rationale: "Which" refers to the plural "bacteria," so the verb must be plural.

B.rationale: The singular verb does not agree with the plural antecedent "bacteria."

D.rationale: "Living" leaves the relative clause without a verb.

hints: What noun does "which" refer to, and is it singular or plural?

strategy.explanation: Find the antecedent of the relative pronoun.

candidates.remember: A relative pronoun takes the number of its antecedent.

revision_history.reason: both blind solvers: "that" could refer to "colonies" or to "a bacterium," so "lives" was also defensible
revision_history.change: sentence rewritten so the only antecedent is the plural "bacteria"

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a signature from Martinez increased what collectors were willing to pay for a pot.
choices.B: Martinez wanted to take credit for the work of other potters at San Ildefonso.
choices.C: collectors could not tell the difference between signed pottery and unsigned pottery.
choices.D: other potters at San Ildefonso had not learned to make black-on-black ware.

candidates.evidence: signed pieces soon drew higher prices than unsigned ones
candidates.explanation: Martinez began signing pots as collectors' interest grew, and signing others' pots would help them only if her name added value for buyers.

B.rationale: The text gives no evidence of that motive; the practice is better explained by what a signature meant to buyers.

C.rationale: If collectors could not tell signed from unsigned pots, a signature would matter little.

D.rationale: The other women made pots that Martinez signed, so this does not follow.

hints: Why would a signature matter to the women whose pots she signed?

strategy.explanation: Connect the signing to the collectors mentioned earlier.

candidates.remember: An inference should be the most reasonable explanation the text supports.

revision_history.reason: blind solver B: the passage never stated that signed pots sold for more, leaving the inference thinly supported
revision_history.change: passage now states that signed pieces drew higher prices
